analysis.one_liner: Caps prescription drug prices at the lowest price charged in other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 20, 2023, and referred to the Senate HELP Committee the same day, the bill never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Department to set a maximum price for every prescription drug, generally pegged to the lowest retail price for that drug in 11 peer countries such as Japan, Germany, Canada, and France. Those caps would apply across Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA coverage, federal employee plans, and Indian Health Service programs. Drug makers would also have to offer the same capped price to uninsured people and people with private insurance, and face civil penalties of five times the amount they overcharged if they didn't comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare, Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries, veterans, military families on TRICARE, federal employees, patients served by the Indian Health Service, and — because the capped price must be offered directly to everyone — uninsured people and privately insured patients who today often pay the full, uncapped list price. All of them would pay no more for a drug than the lowest price charged in countries like Canada, France, or Japan.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, veterans, Medicaid patients, and the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to set an annual reference price for every prescription drug, generally the lowest retail list price found among 11 reference countries (Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Italy, Canada, Australia, Spain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Sweden), and bars the retail list price from going above it.

Applies the price caps across Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA health care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and Indian Health Service programs — covering the drug purchases of tens of millions of Americans.

Goes beyond federal programs: manufacturers must offer the reference price to uninsured individuals and to people with private or employer insurance, so the cap follows patients into the commercial market rather than protecting only government programs.

Backs the cap with real teeth — a civil penalty of five times the difference between what a manufacturer charged and what it would have charged at the reference price — and sends the penalty money to the National Institutes of Health for drug research.

For drugs whose prices can't be found in at least three reference countries, HHS must set a price based on the drug's therapeutic value, patient access, and research and development costs, so no drug escapes the cap.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and other prescription drug manufacturers, whose U.S. revenues would be capped at the lowest price charged in 11 mostly price-regulated foreign markets — both on federal program sales (with a 5x civil penalty for overcharging) and on sales to uninsured and privately insured patients under the mandatory-offer requirement.

drawbacks.text: Pegging U.S. prices to the lowest of 11 foreign systems — many of which negotiate prices through their governments — would substantially cut what drug companies earn in the United States, and the industry's standard objection is that less revenue means less money for developing new medicines. The bill's answer, routing any collected penalties to NIH for research, does not replace the lost private R&D funding.

For any drug whose pricing information or dosage equivalents are not available in at least three reference countries, HHS would set the price itself based on judgments about the drug's therapeutic effect, value, and development costs — giving a federal agency wide, hard-to-appeal discretion over pricing for exactly the newest drugs most likely to fall in that category.

The mandatory-offer requirement applies the cap to all sales, including to private insurers, without any adjustment for the rebates and discounts that already flow through private negotiations — so list prices, not net prices after rebates, become the legal ceiling, which companies argue misrepresents what is actually paid today.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefit is direct and large: Americans pay several times what people in peer countries pay for identical drugs, and this bill makes the foreign price the U.S. ceiling across every major federal program and the entire commercial market. The honest cost is real too: it would slash the revenue drug companies earn in their most profitable market, and it relies heavily on HHS judgment for newer drugs without comparable foreign prices. Whether the savings to patients outweigh any slowdown in drug development is the genuine debate — but the bill never got far enough for that debate to happen, since it died in committee with a single cosponsor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley, joined by Senator Peter Welch as the bill's only cosponsor, introduced S. 2044 on June 20, 2023.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action of any kind was taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, leaving the bill to die in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they continue charging U.S. prices far above what the same drugs cost in Japan, Germany, Canada, and France, with no reference-price cap, no mandatory offer to the uninsured, and no penalty exposure. Patients who would have paid less under the caps are left paying today's prices.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Price Gouging for Medications Act on June 20, 2023.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only senator to do so.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it received no committee action after referral for the remaining 18 months of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: The industry has broadly opposed international reference-pricing proposals, which would cap U.S. drug prices at levels set by foreign health systems, though its activity on this specific bill is not in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no one ever had to go on record for or against; the bill's only two supporters were both Democrats, and opposition was silence rather than a recorded no.

industries.note: The bill forces these companies to sell every drug at the lowest price charged across 11 foreign markets, both to federal programs and directly to all U.S. patients, with civil penalties of five times any overcharge. The same drugs routinely cost several times more in the U.S., which is why the industry's interest here runs directly against patients' pocketbooks.

industries.industry: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Capped list prices would lower what plans, employers, and Medicare and Medicaid pay for drugs. Their gain comes from the same price cuts patients get, so their interest runs alongside the public's here.

The reference prices technically apply to generics too, but generics are already the cheap end of the market, so the practical effect on them is small; their main benefit is that cheaper brand-name competition doesn't change their role.
